newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore aerospace seen gaining from Asian growth.
newsitem.headline: Singapore aerospace seen gaining from Asian growth.

text.p: The Singapore aerospace industry saw record growth last year and is poised for further strides due to improved global demand and strong Asia-Pacific markets, the government said on Wednesday.
A spokesman for the Economic Development Board (EDB) told reporters aerospace industry output rose 10 percent in 1996 to Singapore $1.58 billion.

Asian carriers will place 40-50 percent of an estimated US$150 billion in aircraft orders globally over the next four years, and air travel will continue to grow by more than 7 percent annually for the next 20 years, the EDB said.
During that period, airlines in the region will receive some 35 percent of the world's aircraft deliveries.
By the year 2010, 50 percent of worldwide air traffic will come from the Asia-Pacific region, the EDB added.

"We have actually added a substantial number of new operations in Singapore over the last two years...mainly new companies in the repair and overhaul sector," said Sia Kheng Yok, head of EDB's Aerospace Industry Development Division.
The EDB said the Singapore aerospace industry attracted new and higher value-added investments in 1996. Total investment commitments in the sector in 1996 are expected to reach S$120 million.
These investments should generate a gross value-added of $150 million per year when fully implemented, it said.
The EDB said about 520 additional high value-added jobs will be created in the aerospace industry.
Singapore Technologies Aerospace (STAe), which does 60 percent of its maintenance work on military aircraft and 40 percent on commercial airlines, aimed to reverse its focus.

"Looking at the global trend, the potential for commercial growth is much bigger," said Gary Yeo, deputy president of STAe. He said the company target was 70 percent commercial business in about three years time.
Margins in military aircraft were flattening compared with larger potential profits in the commercial sector, he said.
STAe, which reported losses of $48.4 million and turnover of $480 million in 1995, expected to fare better in 1996.
Yeo said the company anticipated a 1996 turnover of more than $500 million.
Its stronger performance was seen linked to its increasing role in commercial aircraft heavy maintenance, with western airlines that have older fleets farming out more maintenance work.

The EDB projected the Asia-Pacific repair and overhaul market would double within the next decade to become the world's second-largest market worldwide by 2005 and surpass the United States as the biggest market by 2015.
